before: A terrifying man, dressed all in coarse gray, with a great iron shackle on his leg. A man with no hat, with broken shoes, and with an old rag tied around his head. A man who had been soaked in water, covered in mud, cut by stones and flints, stung by nettles, and torn by thorns. He limped, shivered, glared, and growled. His teeth chattered in his head as he seized me by the chin.
after: A fearsome man, all in coarse grey, with a great iron on his leg. A man with no hat, with broken shoes and an old rag tied round his head. A man soaked by water, smothered in mud, lamed by stones, cut by flints, stung by nettles and torn by briars, who limped and shivered and glared and growled, and whose teeth chattered as he seized me by the chin.

before: I pointed to where our village lay, on the flat land among the alder trees, a mile or more from the church.
after: I pointed to where our village lay, inland on the flat ground among the alders and the pollarded trees, a mile or more from the church.

before: "Ha!" he muttered, thinking it over. "Who do you live with — assuming you're allowed to live, which I haven't decided yet?"
after: “Ha!” he muttered, thinking it over. “And who d’you live with, supposing I’m kind enough to let you live? I haven’t made my mind up on that score.”

before: I had topped up the bottle from the tar-water jug. I knew he would be worse later. I shook the table like a spirit medium, through the force of my unseen grip on it.
after: I’d topped up the bottle from the tar-water jug. I knew he would be worse in a moment. I made the table move like a spirit medium of the present day, such was the strength of my unseen grip.

before: My guilty state of mind about the theft I had so unexpectedly gotten away with did not push me toward an honest confession. But I hope there was some trace of good at the bottom of it.
after: My feelings about the theft for which I had so unexpectedly been cleared didn’t move me to come clean. But I hope there were a few dregs of goodness at the bottom of them.

before: I was beginning to remind her that today was Wednesday, when she stopped me with her same impatient gesture.
after: I began to remind her that today was Wednesday, but the fingers of her right hand made the same impatient movement as before and stopped me.

before: I had little luggage to take to London, for not much of my small wardrobe was suited to my new station. But I began packing that same afternoon, and wildly packed up things I knew I would need the next morning, pretending there was not a moment to lose.
after: I had little luggage to take to London. Of the little I owned, very little suited my new station. Still, I started packing that same afternoon, wildly bundling up things I knew I’d need the next morning, on the pretence that there wasn’t a moment to lose.

after: “Mama dear,” lisped the little girl, “baby would have put hith eyeth out.”

before: For several reasons — not least because I didn't clearly know what Mr. Jaggers would be found to be "at" — I said yes. We dived into the City and came up in a crowded police court, where a blood relation (in the murderous sense) of the deceased — the one with the fanciful taste in brooches — was standing at the bar, uncomfortably chewing something. Meanwhile my guardian had a woman under examination, and was striking her, and the bench, and everyone present, with awe. If anybody, of whatever standing, said a word he didn't approve of, he instantly demanded to have it "taken down." If anybody wouldn't make an admission, he said, "I'll have it out of you!" And if anybody did make an admission, he said, "Now I have got you!" The magistrates shivered under a single bite of his finger. Thieves and thief-takers hung on his words in fearful rapture, and shrank when a hair of his eyebrows turned in their direction. Which side he was on I couldn't make out, for he seemed to be grinding the whole place in a mill. I only know that when I crept out on tiptoe, he was not on the side of the bench — for he was making the legs of the old gentleman who presided quite convulsive under the table, by his denunciations of that gentleman's conduct as the representative of British law and justice in that chair that day.
after: For several reasons — not least because I didn't clearly know what Mr. Jaggers would be found to be "at" — I said yes. We dived into the City and came up in a crowded police court, where a blood relation (in the murderous sense) of the deceased — the one with the fanciful taste in brooches — was standing at the bar, uncomfortably chewing something. Meanwhile my guardian had a woman under examination or cross-examination, I couldn’t tell which, and was striking her, and the bench, and everyone present, with awe. If anybody, of whatever standing, said a word he didn't approve of, he instantly demanded to have it "taken down." If anybody wouldn't make an admission, he said, "I'll have it out of you!" And if anybody did make an admission, he said, "Now I have got you!" The magistrates shivered under a single bite of his finger. Thieves and thief-takers hung on his words in fearful rapture, and shrank when a hair of his eyebrows turned in their direction. Which side he was on I couldn't make out, for he seemed to be grinding the whole place in a mill. I only know that when I crept out on tiptoe, he was not on the side of the bench — for he was making the legs of the old gentleman who presided quite convulsive under the table, by his denunciations of that gentleman's conduct as the representative of British law and justice in that chair that day.

before: Things turned out just as Wemmick had predicted. I soon got the chance to compare my guardian's home with his clerk's. My guardian was in his office washing his hands with scented soap when I arrived from Walworth. He called me over and gave me the invitation for myself and my friends that Wemmick had mentioned. "No ceremony," he said. "No dinner dress. No nonsense."
after: Things turned out as Wemmick had predicted. I soon had a chance to compare my guardian’s household with that of his cashier and clerk. When I came into the office from Walworth, my guardian was in his room washing his hands with scented soap. He called me over and gave me the invitation for myself and my friends that Wemmick had told me to expect. “No ceremony,” he stipulated. “No dinner dress, and let’s say tomorrow.” I asked where we were to come, for I had no idea where he lived. I believe it was his general objection to making anything like an admission that prompted his reply: “Come here, and I’ll take you home with me.” I’ll take this opportunity to remark that he washed his clients off him as if he were a surgeon or a dentist. He had a little closet fitted out for the purpose in his room. The scented soap made it smell like a perfumer’s shop. An unusually large roller towel hung inside the door. Whenever he came in from a police court or saw a client out, he washed his hands and wiped and dried them all over that towel. When my friends and I called at six the next day, he seemed to have had a case of a darker complexion than usual, for we found him with his head stuck into the closet, not only washing his hands but bathing his face and gargling his throat. Even when he had done all that and gone all the way round the towel, he got his penknife out and scraped the case from under his nails before putting on his coat.

before: Some people were lurking outside as usual when we stepped into the street, clearly eager to speak with him. But there was something so final about the halo of scented soap surrounding him that they gave up for the day. As we walked westward, he was recognized and greeted by two people, and started on the subjects of capital punishment and flogging. When I challenged his opinions, he defended them thoroughly, then unexpectedly pulled off what felt like a trick, making me argue against my own earlier points.
after: As usual, there were people lurking about when we stepped into the street, plainly anxious to speak to him. But there was something so final about the halo of scented soap round his person that they gave it up for the day. As we walked west, now and then a face in the crowd recognised him. Whenever that happened, he spoke louder to me. Apart from that he never showed the slightest sign that he knew anyone or noticed anyone knew him.

before: He led us to Gerrard Street, Soho, to a house on the south side. It was a rather grand house of its kind, but desperately in need of paint, with dirty windows. He took out his key and opened the door. We all walked into a stone entrance hall that was bare, gloomy, and seldom used. Then up a dark staircase we went to a set of three rooms on the first floor, connected to each other. The front and largest room was barely furnished as a sitting room. The other two rooms were smaller.
after: He took us to a house on the south side of Gerrard Street in Soho. It was rather stately in its way, though sadly in need of paint, with dirty windows. He took out his key and let us into a bare, gloomy stone hall that saw little use. Then up a dark brown staircase we went, into a row of three dark brown rooms on the first floor. There were carved garlands on the panelled walls, and as he stood among them welcoming us, I know what kind of loops I thought they looked like.

before: Dinner was laid in the best of these rooms. The second was his dressing room, the third his bedroom. He told us he rented the whole house but rarely used more of it than we saw. The table was comfortably set — no silver service, of course — and beside his chair stood a large dumb-waiter, stocked with bottles and condiments. Everything had that half-dead, half-alive quality, just like the forced-growth fruit I'd seen at Mr. Pumblechook's shop. The room was so oppressively heated that I couldn't help comparing it to a hothouse.
after: Dinner was laid in the best of the rooms. The second was his dressing room, the third his bedroom. He told us he had the whole house but rarely used more of it than we now saw. The table looked comfortable — no silver, of course — and beside his chair stood a roomy serving stand with an assortment of bottles and decanters and four dishes of fruit for dessert. I noticed throughout the meal that he kept everything within reach and handed it all out himself.

before: There was a bookcase in the room. I could see from the spines that the books were about evidence, criminal law, criminal biography, trials, acts of Parliament, and similar subjects. The furniture was all very solid and good, like his watch chain. It had an official look, though, and there was nothing merely ornamental anywhere. In a corner stood a little table holding a peculiar set: a deadly-looking gun case, a sword in a scabbard, several strange-looking boxes and packages, and two dreadful plaster casts on a shelf above, showing faces with swollen noses. Mr. Jaggers's own tall dark armchair was the most imposing piece in the room.
after: The room held a bookcase. The spines gave me some idea of its contents: evidence, criminal law, lives of criminals, trials, acts of Parliament and the like. Like his watch chain, the furniture was solid and good. Still, it had an official look, and there was nothing in sight that was there merely for decoration. In a corner stood a little table of papers with a shaded lamp. In that respect too he seemed to bring the office home, ready to wheel it out of an evening and get to work.

before: She was a woman of about forty, I supposed — though I may have thought her younger than she was. Rather tall, with a lithe, nimble figure, extremely pale, with large faded eyes and a mass of streaming hair. I couldn't say whether some affliction of the heart made her lips part as if she were gasping, or whether her face simply had that expression. Her knees had a peculiar look, as though they'd been frequently clenched. I noticed that she always had her eyes on her master. I also noticed that Jaggers found something to criticize in her whenever she came near — some trivial thing about the arrangement of the table, the dishes, or the room — to make her show her hands. Whether he intended me to notice these things or not, I couldn't be sure. I noticed them, and Wemmick's words were fresh in my mind.
after: I supposed her to be about forty, though I may have thought her younger than she was. She was rather tall, lithe and quick, extremely pale, with large faded eyes and a mass of flowing hair. I can’t say whether some disorder of the heart made her lips part as if she were out of breath and gave her face that strange look of sudden alarm and flutter. But I know I’d been to see Macbeth at the theatre a night or two before, and her face seemed to shift in a current of fiery air like the faces I had seen rise out of the witches’ cauldron.

before: She set the dish down, touched my guardian quietly on the arm with a finger to signal that dinner was ready, and vanished. We took our seats at the round table. My guardian kept Drummle on one side of him and Startop on the other. It was a noble fish dish that the housekeeper had put on, and it was followed by a joint of equally fine mutton and then an equally fine bird. Sauces, wines, everything we needed stood on the dumb-waiter ready for us. We all seemed to manage the food and drink well, and my guardian took the lead. It was not at all a talkative dinner, and yet it wasn't dull either. He directed the conversation against us whenever it flagged — which it did occasionally, when we grew rather drunk and reckless — and urged the drinks on us, making steady progress toward his goal of getting us thoroughly intoxicated.
after: She set the dish down, touched my guardian lightly on the arm to let him know dinner was ready, and vanished. We sat down at the round table. My guardian kept Drummle on one side of him, with Startop on the other. The housekeeper had brought in a splendid dish of fish. An equally choice joint of mutton followed, then an equally choice bird. Our host handed out sauces, wines, whatever else we wanted, all of the best, from his serving stand. Once they’d gone round the table he always put them back. In the same way he dealt out clean plates and knives and forks for each course and dropped the used ones into two baskets on the floor beside him. No servant but the housekeeper appeared. She brought in every dish, and each time I saw a face rising out of the cauldron. Years later I made a dreadful likeness of the woman by having someone pass behind a bowl of flaming spirits in a dark room. Apart from the flowing hair, the two faces had nothing in common.

before: Having been persuaded to pay close attention to the housekeeper, both by her own striking appearance and by Wemmick's briefing, I noticed that whenever she was in the room she kept her eyes fixed on my guardian. I also noticed that she would remove her hands from any dish she set before him hesitantly, as if she dreaded his calling her back. She was a most docile creature, like the obedient dogs in the happy-family show. But her hands drew my attention, and I compared them with other hands around the table. Her fingers were thin, but strong and muscular, and they bore signs of having been deeply lined and scratched. Mr. Jaggers seemed to notice my watchfulness, for a new and surprising expression appeared on his face — I only noticed it because I was watching closely.
after: Between the housekeeper’s striking appearance and what Wemmick had told me, I paid particular attention to her. Whenever she was in the room she watched my guardian closely. When she set a dish before him she seemed reluctant to take her hands away, as if she dreaded being called back and wanted him to speak while she was still close by, if he had anything to say. I thought I could see in his manner that he knew this and meant to keep her in suspense.

before: Dinner went off cheerfully. Although my guardian seemed to follow subjects rather than start them, I knew he was pulling our weakest traits out of us. I found myself revealing my tendency toward lavish spending, my habit of patronizing Herbert, and my boasting about my great expectations. It was both a mercy and a disgrace that nothing of a tender nature could possibly be confided to this man, though I strongly suspected Herbert of getting dangerously close to admitting some tender feelings about someone.
after: Dinner passed cheerfully. My guardian seemed to follow our lead in the conversation, but I knew he was wrenching the weakest points of our characters out of us. In my own case, my taste for extravagance, for patronising Herbert and for boasting of my great prospects had all come out before I quite realised I had opened my mouth. It was the same with all of us, but especially with Drummle. My guardian had screwed his tendency to make grudging, suspicious digs at the rest of us out of him before the fish was cleared away.

before: It was when we'd reached the cheese, not before, that our conversation turned to our rowing exploits. Drummle was teased about creeping up behind us at night in that slow, amphibious way of his. At this, Drummle informed our host that he greatly preferred our room to our company, and that as for our strength, he could handle any of us with one hand. My guardian was thoroughly pleased with this remark. He told him so and said, "Come! I like that!" Then he called for more wine and leaned back in his chair, biting his forefinger sideways at Drummle.
after: It was later, when we got to the cheese, that we began to talk about our rowing feats and tease Drummle about his habit of coming up behind us at night in that slow, amphibious way of his. Drummle told our host he greatly preferred our absence to our company, that he was more than a match for us in skill, and that in strength he could scatter us like chaff. Somehow, without our seeing how, my guardian got him worked up almost to ferocity over this trifle. He bared his arm and put his hand round it to show us the muscle. Then we all sat there baring and measuring our arms like so many fools.

before: At that moment, the housekeeper was clearing the table. My guardian, taking no notice of her but with the side of his face turned away from her, was leaning back in his chair biting his forefinger and showing an interest in Drummle that I found utterly baffling. Suddenly he clapped his large hand on the housekeeper's, like a trap, as she stretched it across the table. She trembled and turned white, struggling to pull her hand free.
after: The housekeeper was clearing the table. My guardian took no notice of her. He leaned back in his chair with his face turned half away from her, biting the side of his forefinger and showing an interest in Drummle that baffled me. As she stretched her hand across the table, he suddenly clapped his great hand over it like a trap. He did it so suddenly and so smartly that we all stopped in the middle of our foolish contest.

before: He released her hand and turned that wrist face-up on the table. She brought her other hand from behind her and held both out side by side. The second wrist was badly disfigured — deeply scarred, crisscrossed with scars. When she held her hands out, she took her eyes off Mr. Jaggers and turned them watchfully on every one of us in succession. Her demeanor was so quiet that it made the house quiet too. It was like the cases of those dreadful people I'd waited for at the prison gate on my very first morning in London. They had that same look of belonging to the jail, as if they were never to get free of it.
after: He took his hand off hers and turned the wrist palm up on the table. She brought out the other hand from behind her back and held the two side by side. This second wrist was badly disfigured, with deep scars crossing and recrossing it. As she held her hands out she took her eyes off Mr. Jaggers and looked watchfully at each of us in turn.

before: While he said these words in a leisurely, appraising way, she continued looking at each of us in turn. The moment he stopped, she looked at him again. "That'll do, Molly," said Mr. Jaggers, giving her a slight nod. "You've been admired, and you can go." She withdrew her hands, dropped them at her sides, and left the room. Since Mr. Jaggers and Drummle were clearly very well suited to each other, I felt I'd fallen rather into the background during dinner. But now I slipped in a word.
after: As he spoke in that leisurely, appraising way, she went on looking at each of us in turn as we sat round the table. The moment he stopped, her eyes went back to him. “That’ll do, Molly,” Mr. Jaggers said with a slight nod. “You’ve been admired and you can go.” She withdrew her hands and left the room. Mr. Jaggers put the decanters on the table from his serving stand, filled his glass and passed the wine round.

before: "At half past nine, gentlemen," he said, deliberately setting down his glass and hauling out his gold pocket watch by its massive chain, "I am extremely sorry to announce that it's half past nine."
after: “At half past nine, gentlemen,” he said, “we must break up. Please make the most of your time. I’m glad to see you all. Mr. Drummle, I drink to you.”

before: Taking this hint, we all rose to leave. Before we reached the street door, Startop was cheerfully calling Drummle "old boy" as if nothing had happened. But the old boy was so far from responding that he refused even to walk to Hammersmith on the same side of the street. So Herbert and I, who were staying in town, slipped away together and went home through Temple. As we walked, Herbert told me about his Blackfriars adventure, and I told him lightly about Mr. Jaggers's housekeeper. I had no idea then that the topic would ever come back to me, but it came back before long, as everything in life kept coming back.
after: If he meant to bring Drummle out still further by singling him out, he succeeded perfectly. In sulky triumph Drummle treated the rest of us with increasingly offensive contempt until he was quite unbearable. Through every stage Mr. Jaggers watched him with the same strange interest. Drummle actually seemed to give the wine an extra relish for Mr. Jaggers.

before: At this, Startop took him in hand, though with a much better grace than I had shown, and urged him to be a little more agreeable. Startop being a lively, bright young fellow, and Drummle being the exact opposite, the latter was always disposed to resent him as a direct personal insult. He now retorted with some rude remark, and Startop tried to turn the discussion. But Drummle wouldn't hear of it. Startop protested mildly and Drummle scowled heavily at him.
after: At this point Startop took him in hand, with much better grace than I had shown, and urged him to be a little more agreeable. Startop was a bright, lively young fellow and Drummle his exact opposite, so that Drummle always tended to regard him as a personal affront. He made a coarse, clumsy retort, and Startop tried to turn the talk aside with a little joke that made us all laugh. Drummle resented this small success more than anything. Without threat or warning he pulled his hands from his pockets, dropped his round shoulders, swore and snatched up a large glass. He would have thrown it at his opponent’s head if our host hadn’t deftly caught it the instant he raised it.

before: Taking this hint, we all rose to leave. Before we reached the street door, Startop was cheerfully calling Drummle "old boy" as if nothing had happened. But the old boy was so far from responding that he refused even to walk to Hammersmith on the same side of the street. So Herbert and I, who were staying in town, slipped away together and went home through Temple. As we walked, Herbert told me about his Blackfriars adventure, and I told him lightly about Mr. Jaggers's housekeeper. I had no idea then that the topic would ever come back to me, but it came back before long, as everything in life kept coming back.
after: At this hint we all got up to leave. Before we reached the front door, Startop was cheerfully calling Drummle “old boy” as if nothing had happened. But the old boy was so far from responding that he wouldn’t even walk to Hammersmith on the same side of the street. Herbert and I, who were staying in town, watched them go off on opposite sides, Startop ahead and Drummle lagging in the shadow of the houses, much as he used to follow in his boat.

before: Since I was not going home to supper just yet, and since Herbert had hardly enough powder in the barrel for his own supper, I thought I'd leave Herbert there for a moment and run back upstairs to say a word to my guardian. I found him in his dressing room surrounded by his boots, already hard at work washing his hands of us.
after: The front door hadn’t yet closed, so I thought I would leave Herbert there a moment and run back upstairs for a word with my guardian. I found him in his dressing room among his collection of boots, already hard at work washing his hands of us.

before: About a month after that, the Spider's time with Mr. Pocket was up for good. To the great relief of everyone in the house except Mrs. Pocket, he went home to the family estate.
after: About a month later the Spider’s time with Mr. Pocket was up for good. To the great relief of everyone in the house except Mrs. Pocket, he went home to the family hole.

before: "And was that — honor! — the only time you served out in this part of the country?"
after: “And was that — on your honour! — the only time you worked outside in this part of the country?”

before: All the truth of my position came flashing on me. Its disappointments, dangers, disgraces, consequences of all kinds rushed in on me in such a flood that I was carried away and couldn't help myself.
after: The whole truth of my position flashed upon me. Its disappointments, its dangers, its disgraces, every kind of consequence rushed in at once. I went down under the weight of them and had to struggle for every breath.

before: I could not have spoken one word, though it had been to save my life. I stood with a hand on the chair back and a hand on my breast, where I seemed to be suffocating — I stood so, looking wildly at him until I gasped at him with my lips again, and managed to ask him what he had done. Then it was that he began to uncover the appalling truth.
after: I couldn’t have spoken a word to save my life. I stood with one hand on the back of the chair and one on my chest, where I seemed to be suffocating. There I stood, staring wildly at him, until the room began to heave and spin and I clutched at the chair. He caught me, drew me to the sofa and propped me against the cushions. Down he went on one knee before me, bringing that face I now remembered so well, the face I shuddered at, very close to mine.

before: "Yes, Pip, dear boy, I've made a gentleman of you! It's me what has done it! I swore that time, sure as ever I earned a guinea, that guinea should go to you. I swore afterward, sure as ever I got rich you should get rich. I lived rough so that you should live smooth. I worked hard so that you could be above work. What odds, dear boy? Do I tell it, for you to feel an obligation? Not a bit. I tell it, for you to know as that there hunted, mangled dog what you kept life in got his head so high that he could make a gentleman — and, Pip, you're him!"
after: "Yes, Pip, dear boy, I've made a gentleman of you! It's me what has done it! I swore that time, sure as ever I earned a guinea, that guinea should go to you. I swore afterward, sure as ever I speculated and got rich you should get rich. I lived rough so that you should live smooth. I worked hard so that you could be above work. What odds, dear boy? Do I tell it, for you to feel an obligation? Not a bit. I tell it, for you to know as that there hunted dunghill dog what you kept life in got his head so high that he could make a gentleman — and, Pip, you're him!"

before: "Look here, Pip. I'm your second father. You're my son — more to me than any son. I've put away money only for you to spend. When I was a hired-out shepherd in a lonely hut, not seeing a face but faces of sheep till I half forgot what human faces were, I saw yours. I dropped my smoke when I was alone, and I says, 'Here's the boy again, looking at me while I eats and drinks!' I see you there, a many times as plain as ever I see you on them misty marshes. 'Lord strike me dead!' I says each time — and I goes out in the open air to say it under the open heavens — 'but what, if I gets liberty and money, I'll make that boy a gentleman!' And I done it. Why, look at you, dear boy! Look at you!"
after: “Look here, Pip. I’m your second father. You’re my son — more to me than any son. I’ve put money by just for you to spend. When I was a hired shepherd in a lonely hut, never seeing any faces but sheep’s faces till I half forgot what men and women looked like, I saw yours. Many a time I dropped my knife in that hut, eating my dinner or my supper, and I says, ‘Here’s the boy again, looking at me while I eat and drink!’ Many’s the time I saw you there, plain as I ever saw you on them misty marshes. ‘Lord strike me dead!’ I says each time — and I’d go outside to say it under the open sky — ‘if I get my freedom and my money and don’t make that boy a gentleman!’ And I done it. Why, look at you, dear boy! Look at these lodgings of yours, fit for a lord! A lord? Ah! You shall match money with lords for a wager, and beat ’em!”

before: In his heat and triumph, and in his knowledge that I had been nearly fainting, he did not notice my reception of all this. It was the last thing that could have occurred to him, a creature such as he was.
after: In the heat of his triumph, and knowing I had nearly fainted, he didn’t notice how I took all this. That was my one grain of relief.

before: "Don't you mind talking, Pip," he said after again drawing his sleeve over his eyes and forehead, as the click came in his throat that I dreaded so terribly. "You ain't looked slowly forward to this as I have. You wasn't prepared for this as I was. But didn't you never think it might be me?"
after: “Don’t you trouble to speak, Pip,” he said, drawing his sleeve across his eyes and forehead again, with that click in his throat I remembered so well. He was all the more horrible to me for being so much in earnest. “Best thing you can do is keep quiet, dear boy. You haven’t looked forward to this the long way round as I have. You weren’t ready for it like I was. But didn’t you ever think it might be me?”

before: "They shall be yours, dear boy, if money can buy them. Not that a gentleman like you, so well set up as you, can't win them off his own game. But money shall back you! Let me finish what I was going to tell you, dear boy. From that there hut and that there hiring-out, I got money left me by my master (which died, and had been the same as me), and I got my liberty and went for myself. In every single thing I went for, I went for you. 'Lord strike a blight upon it,' I says, whenever it was I went for, 'if it ain't for him!' It all prospered wonderful. As I gave you to understand just now, I'm famous for it. It was the money left me, and the gains of the first few year, what I sent home to Mr. Jaggers — all for you — when he first come after you, agreeable to my letter."
after: "They shall be yours, dear boy, if money can buy them. Not that a gentleman like you, so well set up as you, can't win them off his own game. But money shall back you! Let me finish what I was going to tell you, dear boy. From that there hut and that there hiring-out, I got money left me by my master (which died, and had been the same as me), and I got my liberty and went for myself. In every single thing I went for, I went for you. 'Lord strike a blight upon it,' I says, whatever it was I went for, 'if it ain't for him!' It all prospered wonderful. As I gave you to understand just now, I'm famous for it. It was the money left me, and the gains of the first few year, what I sent home to Mr. Jaggers — all for you — when he first come after you, agreeable to my letter."

before: "And then, dear boy, it was a reward for me, look here, to know in secret that I was making a gentleman. The blood horses of them colonists might fling up the dust over me as I was walking. What do I say? I says to myself, 'I'm making a better gentleman than ever you'll be!' When one of them says to another, 'He was a convict, a few year ago, and is an ignorant common fellow now, for all he's lucky,' what do I say? I says to myself, 'If I ain't a gentleman, nor yet ain't got no learning, I'm the owner of such. All on you owns stock and land. Which on you owns a brought-up London gentleman?' This way I kept myself agoing. And this way I held steady on to my object that I registered in my mind to come back one day and see my boy, and make myself known to him, on his own ground."
after: "And then, dear boy, it was a reward for me, look here, to know in secret that I was making a gentleman. The blood horses of them colonists might fling up the dust over me as I was walking. What do I say? I says to myself, 'I'm making a better gentleman than ever you'll be!' When one of them says to another, 'He was a convict, a few year ago, and is an ignorant common fellow now, for all he's lucky,' what do I say? I says to myself, 'If I ain't a gentleman, nor yet ain't got no learning, I'm the owner of such. All on you owns stock and land. Which on you owns a brought-up London gentleman?' This way I kept myself agoing. And this way I kept my mind fixed on coming back one day and see my boy, and make myself known to him, on his own ground."

before: I tried to collect my thoughts, but I was stunned. Throughout, I had seemed to myself to pay more attention to the wind and the rain than to him. Even now, when he had spoken his last words, I heard them and their echoes in the wind.
after: I tried to collect my thoughts, but I was stunned. All along I seemed to have been listening more to the wind and rain than to him. Even now I couldn’t separate his voice from theirs, though theirs were loud and his was silent.

before: Nothing was needed but this. The wretched man, after loading wretched me with his gold and silver chains for years, had risked his life to come to me, and I held it there in my keeping! If I had loved him instead of loathing him, if attraction had taken the place of repulsion, I could hardly have stared at him with more terror.
after: This was all that was needed! The wretched man, after loading wretched me with his gold and silver chains for years, had risked his life to come to me, and here it lay in my keeping! If I had loved him instead of loathing him, if the strongest admiration and affection had drawn me to him instead of the strongest disgust making me shrink away, it could have been no worse. It would in fact have been better, for then the wish to keep him safe would have come naturally and tenderly to my heart.

before: My first care was to close the shutters, so that no light might be seen from without, and then to close and fasten the door. Meanwhile, he sat with the door open, taking no notice of what I did. When I asked him if he would go to bed, he said yes, but asked me for some items of dressing equipment and a pair of slippers. He further asked that he be allowed to remove his outer coat before lying down. When I left him there, he sat still and silent, his face turned toward me, his heavy brown hand on the arm of the chair.
after: My first thought was to close the shutters so no light could be seen from outside, then to close and fasten the doors. As I did so he stood at the table drinking rum and eating biscuit. To see him there was to see my convict at his meal on the marshes again. I half expected him to bend down at any moment and start filing at his leg.

before: When I had gone into Herbert's room and had shut off any other connection between it and the staircase except through the room where our conversation had taken place, I sat down by the fire. I would have sat longer but could not feel safe there either. In a dazed, grief-stricken way, I looked at the room around me and, finding the place empty and cheerless, went out again to be alone in the corridors.
after: I went into Herbert’s room and closed off every way from it to the staircase except through the room where we had been talking. Then I asked him if he would go to bed. Yes, he said, but could he have some of my “gentleman’s linen” to put on in the morning? I brought it out and laid it ready for him, and again my blood ran cold when he took both my hands in his to say goodnight.

before: I got away from him, without knowing how I did it, and mended the fire in the room where we had been together, and sat down by it, afraid to go to bed. For an hour or more, I remained too stunned to think. It was then beginning to occur to me that I would be in great danger from the man who had put me in this position if I stopped his allowance. All of this slowly sank into me.
after: I got away from him, I don’t know how, stirred up the fire in the room where we had sat together and sat down beside it, afraid to go to bed. For an hour or more I was too stunned to think. Only when I began to think did I begin to take in what a wreck I was, and how the ship I’d sailed in had gone to pieces.

before: Miss Havisham's intentions toward me — all a mere dream. Estella not designed for me. I had only suffered in Satis House as a convenience, a sting for the greedy relations, a model with a mechanical heart to practice on when no other practice was at hand. Those were the first smarts I had. But sharper and deeper than any was this — it was for the convict, guilty of I knew not what crimes, and liable to be taken and hanged, that I had deserted Joe.
after: Miss Havisham’s designs for me, all a mere dream. Estella never meant for me. I had only been tolerated at Satis House as a convenience, a sting for the greedy relations, a dummy with a mechanical heart to practise on when there was nobody else handy. Those were the first stabs of pain. But the sharpest and deepest of all was this: it was for a convict, guilty of I knew not what crimes, liable to be dragged from the very rooms where I sat thinking and hanged at the Old Bailey door, that I had deserted Joe.

before: I would not have gone back to Joe now. I would not have gone back to Biddy now, for any consideration. Simply, I suppose, because my sense of my own worthless conduct toward them was greater than every consideration. No wisdom on earth could have given me the comfort that I should have derived from their simplicity and fidelity. But I could never, never, never undo what I had done.
after: I would not have gone back to Joe now. I would not have gone back to Biddy now, for any consideration. Simply, I suppose, because my sense of my own worthless conduct toward them was greater than every consideration. No wisdom on earth could have given me the comfort that I should have derived from their simplicity and fidelity. But I could never, never undo what I had done.

before: In every gust of wind and rush of rain, I heard pursuers. Twice I could have sworn there was a knocking and whispering at the outer door. With these fears upon me, I began either to imagine or recall that I had had mysterious warnings of this man's approach. That for weeks gone by, I had passed faces in the streets which I had thought like his. That they had first come at me since the stormy nights in November, and had reappeared among the faces in the streets, and that some dread of this coming must have caused me to start so many times.
after: In every furious gust of wind, in every rush of rain, I heard pursuers. Twice I could have sworn there was a knock and a whisper at the outer door. In my fear I began to imagine, or to remember, that I’d had mysterious warnings of his approach. That for weeks I’d passed faces in the street I thought like his. That as he came nearer across the sea, those likenesses had multiplied. That somehow his wicked spirit had sent these messengers to mine, and that now, on this stormy night, he’d kept his word and was with me.

before: Crowding in with these thoughts came the reflection that I had seen him with my childish eyes to be a desperately violent man. That I had heard that other convict accuse him of attempted murder. That I had seen him struggle in the ditch like a wild beast. That I had a reason to believe he had been tried for some capital offense. And that he had been in prison, and had returned to me in the dead of night.
after: Another thought crowded in upon these. With my own childish eyes I had seen him to be a desperately violent man. I had heard the other convict say over and over that he had tried to murder him. I had seen him down in the ditch tearing and fighting like a wild beast. From these memories I drew into the firelight a half-formed fear that it might be unsafe to be shut in there with him in the dead of that wild and lonely night. The fear swelled until it filled the room and drove me to take a candle and go and look at my dreadful burden.

before: He had rolled a handkerchief round his head, and his face was set and lowering in his sleep. But he was asleep, and quietly too, though he had a pistol lying on the pillow. Assured of this, I softly removed the key of his room to my own pocket and turned the lock upon him, then sat down by my fire again and fell asleep before it.
after: He had tied a handkerchief round his head. His sleeping face was set and grim. But he was asleep, and quietly too, though a pistol lay on his pillow. Once I was sure, I quietly slipped the key into the outside of his door and locked him in before I sat down by the fire again. Little by little I slid off the chair and lay on the floor. Even in sleep I had never lost the sense of my misery. When I woke, the church clocks to the east were striking five, the candles had guttered out, the fire was dead, and the wind and rain deepened the thick black darkness.

before: Neither of us spoke of the boat, but we both thought of it. That was clear from our avoidance of the subject, and from our agreeing — without saying so — to measure my recovery in hours, not weeks.
after: Neither of us mentioned the boat, but we both thought about it. You could tell from the care we took to avoid the subject, and from the way we agreed, without agreeing, to count the time before I could use my hands again in hours rather than weeks.

before: Had I given Joe no reason to doubt my loyalty, and to think that as I grew stronger his hold on me would weaken, and that he had better loosen it in time and let me go, before I pulled myself away?
after: Ah! Had I given Joe no reason to doubt my loyalty, to think that prosperity would make me turn cold and cast him off? Had I given Joe’s innocent heart no cause to sense that the stronger I grew, the weaker his hold on me would be, and that he had better loosen it in time and let me go before I tore myself away?
